t2ogxay.name: US-Iran war and Hormuz
t2ogxay.latestHeadline: Iran's president denies nuclear ambitions, says he's ready for talks
t2ogxay.summary: On 2 October, the US sent a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East amid a stalemate in the Iran war. In the first week of October, Iran's oil minister resigned amid an economic crisis, and on 7 October an attacked tanker in the Strait of Hormuz had 11 Indian nationals among its 12 injured crew, according to India's Foreign Ministry. Around 8 to 12 October, attacks on ships near Hormuz intensified, the US military said it disabled a vessel trying to run its blockade of Iran, and efforts to end the war stalled. By 16 October, BBC Verify counted 12 vessels struck in a week, a record, and Brent oil touched $110 as the US issued new Iran-related sanctions.

t139atn9.summary: In early October, The Guardian reported that US authorities had arrested a California man, Greg Lui, for allegedly smuggling $300m worth of computer servers to China. He allegedly used false paperwork to move export-controlled gear from the US to third countries and then on to China. In mid-October, the South China Morning Post reported on a Semiconductor Industry Association report on the US chip supply chain. It found that China accounts for about 5 per cent of the equipment and materials directly supplied to the US chip industry by country of manufacture, but holds over 90 per cent of certain rare earths needed for chipmaking.

Houthi strikes on Jazan and Najran airports in Saudi Arabia wounded three people, and by around 10 October reports described fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis as intensifying. In the days that followed, Trump said he would look at joining Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, a Houthi official warned the US of a "painful response" if it entered the war, and Saudi Arabia struck oil depots near Sana'a. By mid-October, a Houthi missile strike on the Maashiq Palace in Aden killed five people, and the UAE reportedly agreed with Saudi Arabia to re-enter the conflict.

t1rn1bq5.summary: In early October, the euro fell to a 17-month low against the US dollar. Reports linked the drop to concerns about France's ability to bring its public finances in order, and said the currency had lost nearly 7 percent from its peak in late January. At the same time, France's Cac 40 index slid, and the announcement of a snap election in Spain was also reported to be adding to eurozone uncertainty. DW noted that the fall would make inflation worse in the EU, where political worries and concern over French debt were already troubling investors.

t14axxk2.summary: On 5 October, Ukraine's president condemned a Russian strike on a Turkish-owned boat carrying corn in the Black Sea, in which the captain was killed and 11 crew members were rescued. On 6 October, Bulgaria began a search operation after drones hit two ships and the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan sank. On 7 October, Russian authorities said "unmanned boats" attacked a Liberian-flagged tanker off Sochi, sparking a giant fire of oil. By 8 October, France 24 reported that three Turkish-owned cargo ships out of Ukraine had been hit in EU waters by suspected Russian drones, with ten Egyptian and Syrian crew members missing, and on 13 October Bulgaria's prime minister said a drone attack off its coast had sunk a ship and hit two, including the Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, which was damaged.

On October 11, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv was ready to halt refinery strikes if Moscow stopped attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, and US President Donald Trump said both sides had agreed to stop targeting energy infrastructure. By October 16, Zelensky said Ukraine would resume the refinery strikes after having paused them to comply with a US demand, and Russian authorities said Ukraine had struck a major refinery southeast of Moscow in response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Trump called the resumed strikes a "disgrace" that keeps global energy prices elevated.

t12s750z.summary: On October 7, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said big economies would have to make hard choices as soaring bond yields hit budgets. On October 11, Al Jazeera reported that the US-Israel war on Iran and its inflationary impact, along with high debt, would dominate the IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok. By October 12, US Treasury yields had touched 24-year highs as a global bond sell-off picked up, with the 10-year at 5.36% and the 30-year at 5.73%, the highest for each since 2002. On October 13, yields fell as energy prices pulled back, while some analysts said investors were demanding a higher "term premium" to buy government debt, reflecting worries about debt levels and deficits.

CNBC also reported that HSBC and Goldman Sachs expect the RBI to raise rates again in December. In mid-October, CNBC reported that India's retail inflation rose to 5.54% in September, above estimates, marking the 11th straight month of increase.

Minutes released on October 7 showed policymakers had grown increasingly concerned about inflation risks at their September meeting, and on October 8 a top Fed official cast further doubt on a rate rise that month, with any further increase seen as unlikely until the end of the year. t17jq34i.name: IMF global outlook warnings
t17jq34i.latestHeadline: ‘Countries are defying gravity’: how much longer can global economy resist chaos?
t17jq34i.summary: On 13 October, the IMF's World Economic Outlook warned that the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience, with states' oil stocks low and budgets overstretched. The same day, the IMF slightly raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1%, citing the resilience of advanced economies despite rising energy prices caused by the Iran war. Reports on 13 October also said the fund expected persistent conflicts and high energy costs to widen the gap between rich and poor countries, and that Iraq, Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar faced double-digit GDP declines. It also warned of risks from high valuations and debt in the AI sector, government borrowing and cyber-attacks. On 17 October, The Guardian noted that sky-high oil prices and geopolitical turmoil had made less of a dent than feared, but cautioned that this might not last.

events.headline: Russia says Europe bought $320 billion in hydrocarbons since 2022
U.S. Floats Lifeline to Russia: Allowing More Gas Sales to Europe

t1hzeedz.summary: On October 13, Russia said that European Union countries had bought $320.7 billion worth of its energy resources since 2022, despite sanctions over the war in Ukraine. By October 17, The New York Times reported that the Trump administration was pitching the idea of allowing more gas sales from Russia to Europe as part of a peace deal with Ukraine. The report said Europe is wary and critics say Russia would be strengthened.

t1rzjgok.name: US budget deficit and Treasury yields
t1rzjgok.latestHeadline: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge
t1rzjgok.summary: In mid-October 2026, The New York Times reported that the U.S. budget deficit was nearing $2 trillion, with higher interest rates inflating borrowing costs as the Trump administration spent on the Iran war and tariff refunds. The same day, CNBC reported that Treasury yields above 5% were raising borrowing costs for households and the federal government, highlighting the challenge of financing $2 trillion deficits.
